title: git-ai-project/git-ai — A Git extension for tracking the AI-generated code in your repos
content:
Git AI is an open source git extension that tracks the AI-generated code in your repositories. After installing the extension, every line of AI code is linked to the agent, model, and prompts that generated it — so you never lose the intent, requirements, and architecture decisions behind your code.

No per-repo setup or git hooks required. Commit with the Agent, git, or your favorite git client. Attribution will be linked to commits automatically.
The Git AI standard is supported by:
- 🪄 Transparent — Git AI requires no workflow changes. Just prompt and commit as you normally would and Git AI automatically attaches attribution metadata to every commit.
- ⚡ No performance overhead — Git AI does not rely on Git Hooks (slow + difficult to set up in every repo) and it does not wrap the Git binary. Your Git operations are just as fast as they were before Git AI was installed.
- 💻 Local-first — Works offline, no login required.
- 🔒 Secure Prompt Storage — Git AI links each line of AI-code back to the prompt that generated it. These sessions are scanned and redacted, and saved outside of Git -- keeping repos lean, enabling fine-grained access control, and preventing PII or secrets from leaking.
- 🌐 Git native and open standard — Git AI built the open standard for tracking AI-generated code with Git Notes.

report.summary: Git AI is an open-source Git extension that attributes every AI-generated line of code to the exact agent, model, and prompt behind it — with no workflow changes.
report.background: Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, and Devin now write a large and growing share of committed code, but Git records only one author per commit. Teams have no reliable way to know which lines were machine-generated, which model produced them, or what prompt drove them — a blind spot for code review, incident response, security auditing, licensing, and measuring whether AI tooling actually pays off. Earlier approaches tried to 'detect' AI code with heuristics or classifiers, which are inaccurate and easily fooled. Git AI takes the opposite route: agents explicitly report the lines they write, and the extension stores that attribution in Git Notes, an existing Git-native mechanism, so provenance travels with the repository itself.
key_points: Zero workflow change and zero overhead: install once with a single curl or PowerShell command, then commit with any Git client as usual. Git AI deliberately avoids Git hooks and never wraps the Git binary, so Git operations stay as fast as before, and everything runs locally and offline with no login.

Line-level attribution via Git Notes: agents call 'git ai checkpoint' whenever they write code; on commit, attribution is written to Git Notes linked to agent, model, and session. 'git ai blame' is a drop-in replacement for git blame, and 'git log --show-notes="ai"' reveals the metadata.

Attribution survives history rewrites: rebase, squash, merge, reset, stash, and cherry-pick all move and merge line-level attributions, so AI-generated code stays accurately tracked through complex Git workflows — a common failure point for simpler tracking schemes.

Measurable analytics: 'git ai stats --json' reports human vs AI additions, AI lines generated versus accepted, human override rates, and a per-tool/per-model breakdown (for example claude_code/claude-sonnet-4-5), letting teams track AI code from prompt to production.

Accuracy by design, plus privacy controls: Git AI does not use AI or heuristics to guess what is AI-written — agents report exactly which lines they touched. Prompts and sessions are scanned, redacted, and stored outside Git to keep repos lean and prevent secrets or PII from leaking.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Git AI is less a product than a measurement layer: once every line carries an agent and model tag, vendors can be compared on acceptance rates, durability, and rework rather than benchmark hype, and 'AI code provenance' could become a standard artifact alongside SBOMs. For developers, it means honest visibility into how much of a codebase is machine-written, faster review, and the ability to trace a production incident back to the prompt that caused it. For regular users, the benefits are indirect but real — better maintained, more auditable software — though it also normalizes prompt logging and raises uncomfortable questions about AI-attribution data being used in performance reviews, licensing disputes, or blame games. Its main limitation is that coverage depends on agents cooperating.
report.tools: Start with the git-ai CLI (Apache 2.0, usegitai.com) and its IDE plugins for VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Antigravity, and Emacs magit, which color-code lines by agent session and reveal prompts on hover. Pair it with 'git notes' and 'git log --show-notes="ai"' for raw inspection, and 'git ai stats --json' for dashboards. For wider provenance work, look at SPDX 3.0 AI profiles and CycloneDX ML-BOM, plus existing agent analytics in GitHub Copilot metrics and Cursor usage dashboards.
